title: Vending machine (State pattern)
scopeHtml:
Scope: requirements, State pattern with Idle and HasMoney states, runnable Java and Kotlin, session-level locking, follow-ups.

Scope: requirements, State pattern with Idle and HasMoney states, runnable Java and Kotlin, session-level locking, follow-ups.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a vending machine: insert money, pick a slot, get the item and change. The point of this question is the State pattern.

Functional:

  • Slots (codes like A1) each hold a product with a price and a quantity.
  • Insert money (any number of times), select a slot, receive the product and change.
  • Cancel at any time before dispensing and get a refund.
  • Reject: selecting before inserting money, sold-out slot, not enough money, unknown slot.

Non-functional: easy to add states (out of service, maintenance) without editing a giant if.

Worked example. Cola costs 40. User inserts 30, selects A1: error "need 10 more". Inserts 20 (balance 50), selects again: Cola dispensed, change 10, back to Idle. Stock of A1 drops from 1 to 0, so the next purchase fails with "sold out".

Industry examples. Real machines (Crane, Vendo) and payment terminals are state machines; the same shape drives TCP connections (LISTEN, ESTABLISHED, CLOSED), Android MediaPlayer (Idle, Prepared, Started) and order lifecycles at Swiggy or Amazon (placed, paid, shipped).

Everyday analogy. A turnstile: the same push means "nothing" when it is locked and "open" when a coin has been put in.

Common interview traps.

  • Not asking about coin types, card payment or change availability (see Follow-ups).
  • One huge switch(state) in every method; this is what the pattern removes.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Product: name and price.
  • VendingMachine (the context): catalog, stock, current balance, current State.
  • State (interface) with IdleState and HasMoneyState: each implements insertMoney, select, cancel.

The same user action means different things in different states. That is the whole idea: instead of the machine asking "what state am I in?" in every method, it delegates to the state object, and the state object decides and switches the state.

Where the "dispensing" state went. In a real machine dispensing takes seconds and has its own state. Here dispensing is instant, so it is a method (dispense) and we go straight back to Idle. Add DispensingState as soon as it becomes asynchronous (motor, sensor); that is a cheap, reversible change thanks to the pattern.

Decision gravity. State objects hold no data themselves (data lives in the machine), so you can reuse one instance per state. Moving stock into states would be a one-way mess. Money as int in the smallest unit (paise, cents) avoids rounding.

Everyday analogy. A traffic light controller: the controller (machine) is fixed, and the colour (state) decides how it reacts to a "pedestrian pressed button" event.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting balance and stock inside the state objects.
  • Forgetting that cancel must refund and reset to Idle.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+----------------------+
                  | <<interface>> State  |
                  | insertMoney(m, amt)  |
                  | select(m, code)      |
                  | cancel(m): int       |
                  +----------^-----------+
                    |                |
          +-------------+     +----------------+
          | IdleState   |     | HasMoneyState  |
          +-------------+     +----------------+
                  \              /  sets m.state
                   v            v
              +------------------------+        +---------+
              | VendingMachine         |------->| Product |
              |  state: State          | 1..*   | name    |
              |  balance, stock, log   |        | price   |
              |  insertMoney/select/   |        +---------+
              |  cancel -> state.xxx() |
              +------------------------+

 Transitions:
   Idle      --insertMoney--> HasMoney
   HasMoney  --insertMoney--> HasMoney   (balance grows)
   HasMoney  --select OK----> Idle       (dispense + change)
   HasMoney  --cancel-------> Idle       (refund)

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing states as plain strings; the diagram must show who owns the transition.
  • Missing the HasMoney -> HasMoney self loop.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• State. Why: behaviour depends on state and states multiply. Alternatives: an enum with a when in every method (fine for 2 or 3 states and fewer methods; becomes unreadable at 6+). Cost: more classes. Reversible: you can collapse back.
  • Context + delegation. VendingMachine.select() is one line: state.select(this, code). The machine never branches on state.
  • Singleton/flyweight for states. States are stateless so a single shared instance each is fine; we allocate new ones for clarity.
  • Strategy for change-making (optional). Greedy coin selection can be a strategy, see Follow-ups.

Industry examples. Android lifecycle callbacks, Kotlin coroutine state machines (the compiler generates one per suspend function), and Stripe's PaymentIntent (requires_payment_method, processing, succeeded) are all explicit state machines.

Everyday analogy. A bank teller who follows a different checklist depending on whether you have already shown ID.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up State (the object changes itself) and Strategy (the caller chooses). Both use delegation; the difference is who switches.
  • Letting states mutate machine fields in ways that skip validation.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Java (compiled and run with JDK 21):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;

class Product {
    final String name; final int price;
    Product(String name, int price) { this.name = name; this.price = price; }
}

/** State pattern: each state decides what every user action means. */
interface State {
    void insertMoney(VendingMachine m, int amount);
    void select(VendingMachine m, String code);
    int cancel(VendingMachine m);                 // returns refunded amount
}

class VendingMachine {
    final Map<String, Product> catalog = new HashMap<>();
    final Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();
    int balance = 0;
    State state = new IdleState();
    final List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();   // what was dispensed, for tests

    void add(String code, Product p, int qty) { catalog.put(code, p); stock.put(code, qty); }
    void insertMoney(int amount) { state.insertMoney(this, amount); }
    void select(String code) { state.select(this, code); }
    int cancel() { return state.cancel(this); }

    void dispense(String code) {                  // called by states only
        Product p = catalog.get(code);
        stock.merge(code, -1, Integer::sum);
        balance -= p.price;
        log.add(p.name);
        if (balance > 0) { log.add("change " + balance); balance = 0; }
    }
}

class IdleState implements State {
    public void insertMoney(VendingMachine m, int a) {
        if (a <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad amount");
        m.balance += a; m.state = new HasMoneyState();
    }
    public void select(VendingMachine m, String c) { throw new IllegalStateException("insert money first"); }
    public int cancel(VendingMachine m) { return 0; }
}

class HasMoneyState implements State {
    public void insertMoney(VendingMachine m, int a) {
        if (a <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad amount");
        m.balance += a;
    }
    public void select(VendingMachine m, String code) {
        Product p = m.catalog.get(code);
        if (p == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no such slot " + code);
        if (m.stock.get(code) <= 0) throw new IllegalStateException("sold out " + code);
        if (m.balance < p.price) throw new IllegalStateException("need " + (p.price - m.balance) + " more");
        m.dispense(code);
        m.state = new IdleState();                // dispensing done, back to start
    }
    public int cancel(VendingMachine m) {
        int refund = m.balance; m.balance = 0; m.state = new IdleState(); return refund;
    }
}

Kotlin core (hand translated, not compiled in this session). Sealed classes make illegal states unrepresentable and the when exhaustive:

class Product(val name: String, val price: Int)

sealed interface State
object Idle : State
object HasMoney : State

class VendingMachine {
    private val catalog = mutableMapOf<String, Product>()
    private val stock = mutableMapOf<String, Int>()
    var balance = 0; private set
    var state: State = Idle; private set
    val log = mutableListOf<String>()

    fun add(code: String, p: Product, qty: Int) { catalog[code] = p; stock[code] = qty }

    fun insertMoney(amount: Int) {
        require(amount > 0) { "bad amount" }
        balance += amount
        state = HasMoney                                  // Idle and HasMoney both end here
    }

    fun select(code: String) {
        check(state == HasMoney) { "insert money first" }
        val p = requireNotNull(catalog[code]) { "no such slot $code" }
        check(stock.getValue(code) > 0) { "sold out $code" }
        check(balance >= p.price) { "need ${p.price - balance} more" }
        stock[code] = stock.getValue(code) - 1
        log += p.name
        if (balance > p.price) log += "change ${balance - p.price}"
        balance = 0; state = Idle
    }

    fun cancel(): Int { val r = balance; balance = 0; state = Idle; return r }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Decrementing stock before checking the balance, which loses stock on a failed purchase.
  • Throwing a generic Exception; use clear types or a result object.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        VendingMachine m = new VendingMachine();
        m.add("A1", new Product("Cola", 40), 1);
        m.insertMoney(30);
        try { m.select("A1"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("error: " + e.getMessage()); } // need 10 more
        m.insertMoney(20);
        m.select("A1");
        System.out.println(m.log);                       // [Cola, change 10]
        m.insertMoney(50);
        try { m.select("A1"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("error: " + e.getMessage()); } // sold out
        System.out.println("refund " + m.cancel());      // 50

        SafeVendingMachine sm = new SafeVendingMachine();
        sm.add("A1", new Product("Cola", 40), 3);
        ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        List<Future<Boolean>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) fs.add(ex.submit(() -> sm.buy("A1", 40)));
        int ok = 0; for (Future<Boolean> f : fs) if (f.get()) ok++;
        ex.shutdown();
        System.out.println("successful buys = " + ok + ", dispensed = " + sm.dispensed()); // 3, 3
    }
}

Actual output from javac Demo.java && java Demo:

error: need 10 more
[Cola, change 10]
error: sold out A1
refund 50
successful buys = 3, dispensed = 3

Cases covered: not enough money, success with change, sold out, cancel with refund, and 20 threads buying 3 items.

Common interview traps.

  • Not testing the failure paths; most of the logic is there.
  • Forgetting that the failed select must leave the balance intact for the user to add more.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
A vending machine has one user at a time, so the real question is protecting a session. If two threads (a UI thread and a timeout thread that refunds after 60 s idle) call into the machine, per-method locks are not enough: thread A inserts money, thread B inserts money, thread A selects, and A has spent B's coins.

Rule: lock the whole business operation, not individual calls. The safe class below exposes one atomic buy(code, money) that inserts, selects and refunds on failure while holding a ReentrantLock.

/** One user session at a time: a lock around the whole buy, not around single calls. */
class SafeVendingMachine {
    private final VendingMachine m = new VendingMachine();
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

    void add(String code, Product p, int qty) {
        lock.lock(); try { m.add(code, p, qty); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
    boolean buy(String code, int money) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            m.insertMoney(money);
            try { m.select(code); return true; }
            catch (IllegalStateException e) { m.cancel(); return false; }   // refund on failure
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
    int dispensed() {
        lock.lock();
        try { return (int) m.log.stream().filter(s -> s.equals("Cola")).count(); }
        finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

Gravity. A single lock is correct and cheap here (one machine, low QPS). A per-slot lock only helps if many users could buy at once, which a physical machine cannot. For a networked fleet (thousands of machines reporting stock) the contention is in the stock database, solved with a conditional update UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1 WHERE slot=? AND qty>0.

Symptom in production. Stock goes negative or the display says 0 while a cola drops: a lost update. The metric: stock below zero in the backend.

Everyday analogy. One counter at a post office: only one person is served from start to finish; a second person cannot slip in between "hand over form" and "get stamp".

Common interview traps.

  • Synchronizing each method but not the sequence insert, select.
  • Holding the lock while doing slow hardware work with no timeout.
  • Using a non-reentrant lock and then calling one locked method from another.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Card/UPI payment. A PaymentMethod strategy; the state HasMoney becomes "Authorized".
  • Not enough change. Track coin inventory; make change with a greedy coin strategy (works for canonical coin sets like 1, 2, 5, 10; use DP otherwise) and reject the sale if exact change is impossible.
  • Out of service. Add OutOfOrderState that rejects everything; no edits to other states.
  • Restock/admin mode. A separate admin API behind a key, not the user API.
  • Timeout refund. A scheduler calls cancel after N seconds in HasMoney; this is exactly where the lock matters.

Common interview traps.

  • Hard-coding coin denominations in the state classes.
  • Ignoring the failure when the motor jams after charging: you need a compensating refund.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Requirements: slots, insert, select, change, cancel, with clear error cases.
  • State pattern: Idle and HasMoney objects decide what each action means and switch the machine's state; no giant switch.
  • Money is an int in the smallest unit; check stock and balance before changing anything.
  • Concurrency: lock the whole session (insert, select, refund), not single calls; in a fleet use a conditional stock update in the database.
  • Easy extensions: new states, payment strategies, change-making strategy.

questions.promptHtml: Why model a vending machine with the State pattern instead of one class with if (state == ...) in every method? Walk through the transitions.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The vending machine is the standard State-pattern question; they check you can say what the pattern removes and where the transition lives.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The same user action means different things in different states: inserting money in Idle starts a session, selecting in Idle is an error, selecting in HasMoney dispenses. With State, the machine delegates each action to the current state object and that object decides and switches the state, so there is no growing switch in every method. Adding a state such as out-of-service is a new class, not edits in five methods.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Idle      --insertMoney--> HasMoney
HasMoney  --insertMoney--> HasMoney   (balance grows)
HasMoney  --select OK----> Idle       (dispense + change)
HasMoney  --cancel-------> Idle       (refund)

VendingMachine.select(code) is one line, state.select(this, code). The machine owns the data (catalog, stock, balance); the states own only behaviour. That is why one shared instance per state is possible. The cost is more classes; for 2 or 3 states and few methods an enum with when is also fine, so say when you would switch back.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing balance or stock inside state objects.
  • Forgetting the HasMoney -> HasMoney self loop.
  • Forgetting that cancel must refund and reset to Idle.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where is dispensing in the diagram? -> It is a method called by HasMoneyState because it is instant here; add DispensingState when it becomes asynchronous (motor, sensor).
  2. Who is allowed to change state? -> Only the state objects (or a package-private setter); callers never do.
  3. Show the enum alternative and its limit. -> when (state) in each of insert/select/cancel; at 6+ states and 5+ actions that is 30 cells to keep consistent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "State avoids if/else". The senior states what stays in the context (data), that transitions are owned by states, and when the pattern is overkill.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Order lifecycles (placed, paid, shipped, returned) in commerce back ends are exactly this shape; a payment intent stuck in the wrong state is the usual bug.

questions.promptHtml: State and Strategy have the same class diagram. What is the real difference, and which one is the vending machine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A common trap question; it tests whether you understand intent, not structure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both delegate to an interface. In Strategy the caller picks the algorithm and it does not change by itself (pricing rule, spot choice). In State the object switches its own behaviour as it moves through a lifecycle, and the state objects know about each other. The vending machine is State: the state decides what the next state is. Change-making for coins is a Strategy inside it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strategy:  Client -> Context -> Strategy      (client chose it, stays until client changes it)
State:     Client -> Context -> State -> sets Context.state = NextState   (self-driven)

Test of the difference: ask "who calls the setter?". Strategy: the wiring code. State: the behaviour itself. Strategy objects are usually interchangeable and ignorant of each other; State objects form a graph of transitions.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
the only line that makes it State is the transition inside the state class:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public int cancel(VendingMachine m) {
    int refund = m.balance; m.balance = 0;
    m.state = new IdleState();                 // the state switches the machine itself
    return refund;
}
override fun cancel(m: VendingMachine): Int {
    val refund = m.balance; m.balance = 0
    m.state = IdleState                          // the state switches the machine itself
    return refund
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "State has more classes" as the difference.
  • Letting states mutate machine fields in ways that skip validation.
  • Calling a PaymentMethod interface a State.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can one design use both? -> Yes: HasMoneyState.select calls a ChangeStrategy to make change.
  2. Can state objects be shared? -> If they hold no data, one instance each (flyweight); allocating new ones is only for clarity.
  3. How do sealed classes help in Kotlin? -> Exhaustive when over a sealed state type makes a missing state a compile error.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "they look the same". Senior: who switches, lifetime, and the example of both in one machine.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that modelled a retry policy as State had it flip by itself at runtime; it was a Strategy and should have been chosen by configuration.

questions.contextHtml:
Customers say: "I put in 30, chose Cola (40), it said need 10 more, and the slot count dropped anyway." After three such attempts the slot shows sold out with 3 colas physically inside.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public void select(VendingMachine m, String code) {
    Product p = m.catalog.get(code);
    m.stock.merge(code, -1, Integer::sum);                  // reserve the item
    if (m.stock.get(code) < 0) throw new IllegalStateException("sold out " + code);
    if (m.balance < p.price) throw new IllegalStateException("need " + (p.price - m.balance) + " more");
    m.dispense(code);
    m.state = new IdleState();
}
fun select(code: String) {
    val p = catalog[code]!!
    stock[code] = stock.getValue(code) - 1                   // reserve the item
    check(stock.getValue(code) >= 0) { "sold out $code" }
    check(balance >= p.price) { "need ${p.price - balance} more" }
    dispense(code); state = Idle
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you restructure so that a failed purchase changes nothing?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds stock++ in a catch block. That patches one path and leaves unknown slots (NPE) and the sold-out path inconsistent.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should a failed select keep the balance so the user can add more (yes, per requirements)? Is the exception the only error channel?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reconcile stock by a physical count and fix the data; ship the reorder fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Mutation before validation; sold-out check happens after the decrement (stock goes to -1 on a sold-out try); unknown slot gives NPE from catalog.get.
  4. How I'd verify each: Tests: not enough money leaves stock and balance unchanged; sold out leaves stock at 0 not -1; unknown slot raises a clear error.
  5. Root cause: Validation and mutation interleaved; a failure halfway leaves partial state.
  6. Fix: Validate everything first (slot exists, stock > 0, balance >= price), then mutate in one step inside dispense. Rule: validate, then commit.
  7. Prevention: A test per failure path asserting full state equality before and after; reviewers look for any write before the last check.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not wrap in try/catch compensation for in-memory validation; compensation is for real side effects such as a jammed motor, where a refund is needed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Motor jams after the stock was decremented? -> Mutate stock only after the hardware confirms, or compensate with a refund and mark the slot faulty.
  • Generic Exception thrown? -> Use typed errors or a result object so the UI can show a precise message.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A kiosk decremented inventory before payment confirmation; every declined card shrank the visible stock until the slot looked sold out.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: catch-and-restore patch.
  • Hire: validate first, commit once, tests for failures.
  • Strong hire: also covers the hardware-failure compensation and state-equality tests.

questions.contextHtml:
The machine now has a UI thread and a scheduler thread that calls cancel() after 60 s idle in HasMoney. Each method of VendingMachine is individually synchronized. Field report: a customer inserted 20, then 20 more, selected Cola (40) and got "need 40 more" and a refund of 0; another got a Cola and a refund of their 20 as well.

t=59.98s  UI:        insertMoney(20)  -> balance 40
t=59.99s  scheduler: cancel()         -> refund 40, balance 0, state Idle
t=60.00s  UI:        select("A1")     -> state Idle: "insert money first"
questions.promptHtml: Why are per-method locks not enough, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make everything synchronized" (already so), or "increase the timeout".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the timer restarted on each coin? Can the user cancel from the keypad as well? How long may a lock be held (hardware calls)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reset the idle timer on every action and make the timeout check "idle for 60 s since last activity" under the same lock.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A session is a sequence (insert, insert, select) but the lock only covers single calls, so another thread interleaves between steps. Second: the timeout's decision is based on a stale read. Red herring: the synchronized keyword is present on all methods, which hides the bug in review.
  4. How I'd verify each: Deterministic test with an injected scheduler (run the timeout between steps); log session id on each call.
  5. Root cause: The invariant "a session runs as one unit" is wider than one method.
  6. Fix: One ReentrantLock around the whole business operation, and the timeout re-checks the last-activity timestamp inside the lock before refunding. A buy(code, money) operation that does insert, select and refund-on-failure atomically for the single-call API.
  7. Prevention: Tests that fire cancel between every pair of steps.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: One lock is right for one physical machine with one user. I would not do per-slot locks (nothing to parallelise) and I would not hold the lock during slow motor work without a timeout.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why a ReentrantLock and not synchronized? -> tryLock(timeout) so a stuck hardware call cannot block the scheduler forever; reentrancy lets locked methods call each other.
  • Is cancel after select completed harmless? -> Yes, state is Idle and balance 0: returns 0.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A kiosk refunded half-finished sessions every night at the same minute because the idle timer was a global cron, not per session.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more synchronized keywords.
  • Hire: lock the whole session and re-check the idle time inside it.
  • Strong hire: deterministic test with injected scheduler and tryLock rationale.

questions.contextHtml: Product adds: (1) an out-of-service mode (door open, sensor fault) where nothing is accepted, (2) a dispensing step that takes 3 s with a motor and may jam, and (3) card/UPI payment alongside coins.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change or are added, and which stay untouched? How do you keep the transition rules explicit?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds boolean flags outOfService and dispensing to VendingMachine and checks them at the top of every method.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: On a jam, refund or retry? Can a user insert coins while dispensing (reject)? Who sets out-of-service (sensor, admin, both)? Does card payment authorise before select?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; extend under existing tests.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The State pattern was chosen for exactly this; new states are new classes.
  4. How I'd verify each: One transition table test per state: every action in every state has an expected result.
  5. Root cause (design): n/a, a planned extension.
  6. Fix: Add OutOfOrderState (rejects everything; cancel refunds if balance > 0), DispensingState (rejects insert and select; on motor success go Idle, on jam go to a refund then OutOfOrder), and PaymentMethod strategy (coin, card) where HasMoney becomes "Authorized" for card. IdleState, HasMoneyState change only where they must know the next state. VendingMachine data unchanged.
  7. Prevention: The transition table as a test; for Kotlin a sealed state type gives an exhaustive when.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More classes, but each is small. I would not add boolean flags: 3 flags give 8 combinations of which most are illegal.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Motor jams after charging a card? -> Compensating refund (reverse the authorisation) before moving to OutOfOrder; this is a saga, not a rollback.
  • Admin restocks while a user is mid-session? -> A separate admin API behind a key that requires Idle, not mixed into the user API.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A machine with a maintenanceMode boolean accepted coins in maintenance because one new method forgot to check it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: boolean flags.
  • Hire: new State classes, payment strategy, unchanged data holder.
  • Strong hire: compensation on jam, transition-table test, rejects flag explosion with the count.

questions.contextHtml:
The machine holds coin inventory. Coin set in market A is 1, 2, 5, 10. Market B adds a locally issued set 1, 3, 4. An engineer implements greedy change (largest coin first). A user pays 10 for an item costing 4: change 6 in market B.

Greedy gives 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins); the optimal is 3 + 3 (2 coins). Worse, with only one 4-coin and one 1-coin left, greedy fails to make 6 even though 3 + 3 exists.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do about change-making, and what does the machine do when exact change is not possible?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Greedy always works" or hard-codes denominations in the state classes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the denomination set fixed per market? Does coin inventory matter (limited counts)? Is the fewest-coins goal required or only feasibility?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reject sales whose change cannot be made ("exact change only") rather than keeping the money.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Greedy is correct only for canonical coin systems such as 1, 2, 5, 10; not for 1, 3, 4. Inventory limits break canonical systems too.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit tests with the 1, 3, 4 set and limited counts; brute force comparison for amounts up to 100.
  5. Root cause: An algorithm assumption (canonical system) baked into the code.
  6. Fix: A ChangeStrategy interface. GreedyChange for canonical sets, DpChange (min coins, bounded counts) for the rest, chosen by configuration. Check feasibility before dispensing the product: compute change first; if null, refuse the sale and refund.
  7. Prevention: Property test: result sums to the amount and respects the inventory.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: DP is O(amount x coin types), trivial for amounts under a few hundred; I would not ship DP everywhere if greedy is proven correct for the market, because simple code wins.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can DP handle limited coin counts? -> Yes, bounded knapsack style (iterate counts, or expand coins), still small here.
  • Where is the check in the State flow? -> In HasMoneyState.select before dispense, so a failed change leaves state and stock untouched.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A machine took bank notes and then could not make change; it kept the overpayment because nobody had designed the "cannot make change" branch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: assumes greedy.
  • Hire: shows the counterexample and a ChangeStrategy.
  • Strong hire: validates before dispensing, bounded counts, property test.

questions.contextHtml:
5,000 networked machines report sales to a backend that keeps remaining stock per slot and also accepts a mobile "reserve and pay" feature. Mobile reserves allow 2 users to reserve the last Cola from the same machine. Backend stock for one slot reads -2. Peak is 300 reservation requests per second fleet-wide; each machine slot gets under 1 per minute normally, but a promotion sends 40 requests per second to 3 machines.

SELECT machine_id, slot, qty FROM stock WHERE qty < 0;
-- m-0412  A1  -2

The code: qty = SELECT qty ...; if (qty > 0) UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 ....
questions.promptHtml: Why can the quantity go negative, and what is the right design for reserve, expiry and a jammed motor?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Wraps the read-then-update in a Java synchronized method (only one app server, so it fails on the second), or locks the whole table.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is stock reserved before payment or after? How long does a reservation hold? What does the machine report back on dispense? Single region DB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add CHECK (qty >= 0) so the bad write fails loudly, and cap promotion traffic per machine.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Read-then-write without atomicity (lost check). Two backends race. Machine-side sale not synchronised with reservations. Red herring: the 300/s fleet-wide rate is low; contention is on 3 hot rows.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay with two sessions in the DB; look at the transaction log timestamps of the two decrements.
  5. Root cause: Check-then-act across a network boundary.
  6. Fix: Single conditional statement: UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE machine_id=? AND slot=? AND qty > 0 and use rows-updated = 1 as the success signal. Reservations are rows with expiry (reserved_until) and the stock decrements at reserve; an expiry sweeper increments back; a jam produces a compensating refund and a faulty flag on the slot. The machine's own local session lock stays (one user at a time).
  7. Prevention: CHECK constraint, a reconciliation job comparing backend stock with machine counts, alerts on negative or drifting stock.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The hot-row throughput is limited by one row lock, about hundreds of updates per second per row, which is above 40/s, so no sharding needed (verify on your DB). I would not use a distributed lock service for a one-statement problem.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Promotion to 5,000 requests per second on one machine? -> Reservation queue per machine, since only a handful of items exist; reject early with a sold-out flag in cache.
  • Reservation expired but the user arrives? -> The reserve must be extended or re-validated; the conditional update decides again.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promotion oversold a single machine by 11 items; the incident review found a SELECT then UPDATE written in the first version and never revisited.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: language-level lock.
  • Hire: conditional update with rows-updated check.
  • Strong hire: expiry, compensation for jams, reconciliation, correct hot-row reasoning.

questions.contextHtml: A PR adds timeout refunds. The test uses Thread.sleep(61_000) and runs in CI 40 times per day; it fails 1 in 20 runs. A reviewer also asks you for tests of "motor jams after charging" and "20 threads buy 3 items".
questions.promptHtml: How do you restructure for testability and which cases do you cover?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps the sleep and lengthens it, or says "I would test it manually".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the scheduler abstract or java.util.Timer directly? Is the clock System.currentTimeMillis inside the machine?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Quarantine the flaky test; do not delete the coverage.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Real time in tests makes them slow and racy; the scheduler and the hardware are hidden dependencies.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the test 200 times in a loop to measure the flake rate.
  5. Root cause: Time and hardware are not injected.
  6. Fix: Inject a Clock or a Scheduler interface (fake advances manually), and a Motor interface (dispense(slot): Boolean) with a fake that fails. Cases: not enough money; success with change; sold out; unknown slot; cancel refund; timeout refund fires exactly once; motor jam leads to refund and OutOfOrder; failed select leaves balance intact; concurrency: 20 threads buying 3 items gives exactly 3 successes and 3 dispensed.
  7. Prevention: No sleep or real clock in unit tests; a CI rule that fails on Thread.sleep in test sources.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Fakes need maintenance but make tests instant and deterministic; I would not use Mockito for everything where a hand-written fake is clearer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you assert the concurrency test is meaningful? -> Use a start latch so threads begin together and run the loop many times; assert the invariant (stock never negative, successes equal initial stock).
  • Why test failure paths first? -> Most of the logic lives there.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A suite with 14 sleeps took 9 minutes; replacing them with a fake clock cut it to 6 seconds and the flake rate to zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: longer sleep.
  • Hire: injected clock and motor, lists the failure cases.
  • Strong hire: latch-based concurrency test with invariants and the CI rule against sleeps.
